title: The thermodynamic budget of objectivity
problem: Quantum Darwinism explains objective classical facts by redundancy: the environment that decoheres a system broadcasts many records of its pointer observable, so many observers can learn it independently. Records are physical, and making, keeping and destroying them costs energy. The quantum-thermodynamics roadmap lists as open whether there is a thermodynamic price for the emergence of classicality. What is the work needed to create objectivity at a given redundancy and quality, the power needed to keep it, and the speed at which it can emerge?
result: In a minimal broadcast model, a driven qubit writing into \(N\) thermal qubit registers, creating \(R\) records of an event at information deficit \(\delta\) requires work \(W\ge Rk_BT\ln2\,(1-\delta)H(\varepsilon)\), attainable for uniform events. Recording in a basis misaligned by \(\theta\) is impossible at any work beyond \(\theta_c=2\arcsin\sqrt{H_2^{-1}(\delta)}\). Reducing redundancy needs access to \(R-R_{\min}+1\) records but no work, and erasing accessed perfect records yields work. Maintenance against relaxation at rate \(\gamma\) costs power linear in \(R\gamma\), and independently written records obey \(\Sigma A\ge R^2(1-2e^*)^2/2\).
significance: The paper gives a quantitative answer to the roadmap's question, within a stated model class: classicality has a Landauer-rate creation cost linear in redundancy, a steady maintenance cost, and a speed limit set by dissipation times bath activity. It also separates two notions of undoing a fact: redundancy can be thinned silently, while erasing correlation with the event dissipates at least the information removed. The pointer basis appears as the basis that minimizes the work of objectivity.
limitations: All statements are exact only inside a specific model class: qubit registers, controlled unitaries diagonal in the system's basis, ideal thermal contacts and, for the speed limit, scheduled drives without feedback or register–register gates. The paper shows that such gates can beat the speed limit by creating correlated records, and leaves the collective and coherent cases open. Many proofs are given in outline in a short text. The instrument applications rely on the author's companion papers, one of them unpublished.

description: The event is a bit \(\varepsilon\) stored in a system qubit, and the environment is split into fragments \(E_1,\ldots,E_N\). A fragment holds a record at deficit \(\delta\) if its accessible information about \(\varepsilon\) is at least \((1-\delta)H(\varepsilon)\). Objectivity at \((R,\delta)\) means at least \(R\) disjoint fragments hold such records. The registers start thermal, and a work source may apply any controlled unitaries diagonal in the system's \(z\) basis between thermal contacts; forbidding rotations of the system is what makes \(z\) the basis of the recording machinery.

Creation: thermal registers minimize local free energy, so the work of any protocol is at least \(k_BT\) times the correlation it creates, and total correlation dominates the sum of per-fragment informations. Each record therefore costs at least \(k_BT\ln2\,(1-\delta)H(\varepsilon)\), with no saving from collective encodings. Quasistatic reset-then-copy protocols attain this for uniform events. For biased events a perfect record still costs a full \(k_BT\ln2\), because orthogonal conditional register states carry the whole bit regardless of the event's entropy.

Misalignment: every allowed operation commutes with dephasing of the system in \(z\), so records of an event stored in a basis rotated by \(\theta\) hold at most \(1-H_2(\sin^2(\theta/2))\) bits. Beyond \(\theta_c\) the deficit cannot be met, and below it the optimal work rises from \(1-\delta\) to a full bit per record at \(\theta_c\). Undoing: with access to \(k\) perfect records of a uniform bit, a CNOT consolidates two into one at zero work, and the \(k-1\) parities can be extracted as \((k-1)k_BT\ln2\) of work while all \(k\) records are erased; what the second law constrains is the destroyed correlation, not the work.

Maintenance and speed: a record relaxing at rate \(\gamma\) stays within deficit for \(t_{\rm hor}=\gamma^{-1}\ln[(1-2e_0)/(1-2e^*)]\), and holding it indefinitely costs at least \(Rk_BT\ln2\,\gamma\,g(\delta)\), with \(g\) diverging as \(\delta\to0\). At zero gap a thermal register is invariant under every permutation, so unitaries alone create no record; every record is written through the bath. A classical speed limit then bounds the product of entropy production and dynamical activity, so the rate of creating records is at most \(\sqrt{2\bar\sigma\bar a}/(1-2e^*)\). The paper applies the accounting to a calorimeter and to an adiabatic drift filter in which an \(18.6\) keV electron radiates about \(0.66\) meV as about nine microwave photons.

methods.technique: Counting work through correlation with thermal registers
methods.explanation: A lower bound on the work of creating records must hold for every protocol, including collective ones. The free energy of the final state above thermal separates into local terms, which are nonnegative because thermal states minimize local free energy, and a correlation term, which is what the records are.
math: For a protocol that leaves the system's own record intact, the paper derives \[W\ge k_BT\Bigl[\sum_iI(\varepsilon{:}E_i)+I_{\rm fin}(\varepsilon{:}S)-H(\varepsilon)\Bigr],\] with entropies in nats. Requiring \(R\) fragments with \(I(\varepsilon{:}E_i)\ge(1-\delta)H(\varepsilon)\ln2\) and \(I_{\rm fin}(\varepsilon{:}S)=H(\varepsilon)\ln2\) gives \(W\ge Rk_BT\ln2\,(1-\delta)H(\varepsilon)\), linear in redundancy at the Landauer coefficient.

For an event recorded in a basis rotated by \(\theta\), dephasing in \(z\) acts on the event as a binary symmetric channel with flip probability \(q=\sin^2(\theta/2)\). Mrs. Gerber's lemma then forces each fragment to carry at least \(1-H_2(e_1^*)\) bits of correlation with the dephased bit, with \[e_1^*=\frac{e^*-q}{1-2q},\qquad e^*=H_2^{-1}(\delta),\] so \(W=Rk_BT\ln2\,[1-H_2(e_1^*)]\). Editorial check: \(e_1^*\) composed with flip probability \(q\) gives \(e^*\) exactly; at \(q=e^*\), the critical angle, \(e_1^*=0\) and the work is one full bit per record; at \(\theta=0\) it is \(1-\delta\).
methods.transfer: The same decomposition prices any task defined by required correlations with thermal memories, such as distributing a classical key to many registers or maintaining a redundant classical memory.

methods.explanation: One might expect undoing a fact to cost the Landauer price of every record. Redundant records are correlated with one another, and correlation among accessed registers is free energy that an adversary can extract while erasing them.
math: For \(k\) perfect copies of a uniform bit, applying CNOTs from the first copy leaves \(k-1\) registers in a pure state, each worth \(k_BT\ln2\), so an adversary extracts \(W_{\rm ext}=(k-1)k_BT\ln2\) while erasing all \(k\) records, at entropy production \(\ln2\). The event-inclusive entropy production for the controlled sector \(A\) obeys \[\Sigma_{\varepsilon A}=\Sigma_A+\bigl[I_{\rm i}(\varepsilon{:}A)-I_{\rm f}(\varepsilon{:}A)\bigr],\] the second law with information exchange, so full erasure of perfect records dissipates at least \(H(\varepsilon)\), while consolidation destroys no correlation and dissipates nothing.

Editorial check for noisy records: two records with independent flip probability \(0.1\) have joint distribution \((0.41,0.41,0.09,0.09)\), entropy \(1.1645\) nats, and conditional entropy \(2h(0.1)=0.6502\) nats given the event. Discharging them to full mixture extracts \(k_BT(2\ln2-1.1645)=0.222\,k_BT\), and the mutual information destroyed is \(1.1645-0.6502=0.514\) nats, matching the paper's values.
methods.transfer: The access-versus-work distinction applies to any redundant classical storage: protecting a replicated record is a matter of limiting access, because given access, the redundancy itself pays for its own erasure.
